question.text: Government Securities (G-Secs) are often called "gilt-edged securities" because they carry:

answer.text: The highest coupon rate among all debt instruments
Tax-free status on both interest and capital gains
Virtually no risk of default as they are backed by the government
Guaranteed returns that are always higher than inflation

explanation.text: The Logic: The workbook states that government securities do not carry default risk because the government guarantees the payment of interest and the repayment of principal. That sovereign guarantee is the reason G-Secs are described as "gilt-edged" securities. The Trap: "Highest coupon rate" is wrong because G-Sec coupon rates are generally lower than corporate bond yields precisely because of their safety. "Tax-free" is wrong because only specific issues (such as certain PSU tax-free bonds) carry that feature. "Returns always higher than inflation" is wrong because real returns on G-Secs can be negative during high-inflation periods. Note: G-Secs are the closest benchmark when investors ask for "risk-free" instruments, but they still carry interest rate risk and inflation risk -- only the default/credit risk component is essentially eliminated by the sovereign guarantee.
